title: Why Vérone Mankou Built Websites Before He Built a Tablet
dek: In Brazzaville, Vérone Mankou ran an IT services firm to save for the tablet he wanted to make, and in January 2012 the Way-C went on sale.

story.event: Saving through an IT services firm to design the Way-C tablet in Congo and have it assembled in China
story.summary: Vérone Mankou began planning a cheap computer in 2006 while working at an internet service provider in the Republic of the Congo, and turned the idea into a tablet after the first iPhone appeared. He ran VMK as an IT services firm to build reserves, spent most of its budget designing the Way-C, had it assembled in China, and put it on sale in Brazzaville and Pointe-Noire on 30 January 2012.
paragraphs: In 2006 Vérone Mankou was working at an internet service provider in the Republic of the Congo and, he later said, wanted to design a cheap computer that would let more people get online. About a year later Steve Jobs unveiled the first iPhone, and Mankou changed the plan. The project became what he called a "big iPhone": a tablet.

Funding, he said, was hard to find in Congo and across sub-Saharan Africa. So he did not start with the tablet. He started VMK in Brazzaville as an IT services firm, designing websites and applications and consulting, because that was easier to fund. In June 2011 he told TechCentral, "It's taken me two years to get sufficient reserves together to start this project." He knew the price. Asked by the Cameroonian site Ingenieris whether VMK was profitable, he laughed and said it could have been "if I had not had the idea to launch a tablet", which was taking about 80% of the budget.

Congo had no factory that could build the device, so he chose to design it there and have it assembled in China. Early prototype photos read "Designed and Engineered in Congo by VMK"; by May 2011 they read "Designed in Congo. Assembled in China." Doubts followed. Global Voices found a Shenzhen retailer selling a similar tablet for about half the price, and a Congolese journalist said anyone could change a tablet's logo. Mankou answered that he had designed the hardware himself, with a friend in Canada and a partner in Asia working on the software, and that the higher price paid for after-sales service and a presence in Congo.

The Way-C, a name meaning "the light of the stars" in a northern Congolese dialect, was first shown in public in September 2011. On Monday 30 January 2012 it went on sale in Airtel shops in Brazzaville and Pointe-Noire for 150,000 CFA francs, about $300. AFP put the cost of the project since 2006 at more than 80 million CFA francs, essentially provided by VMK. Later that year VMK unveiled a smartphone, the Elikia, Lingala for "hope". In July 2015 it opened a unit to assemble its phones in Congo; Reuters reported that it then employed 200 people.

quote.text: You are unjust, then, and unreasonable if you are unwilling to pay the price for which these things are sold, and would have them for nothing.
quote.source_title: The Enchiridion, tr. Thomas Wentworth Higginson, Project Gutenberg eBook #45109
quote.connection: Mankou said openly what the tablet cost: two years of reserves, most of a budget and the profit VMK might have made. Epictetus, writing about favours bought with flattery, makes the wider point that everything has a price, and you cannot keep the price and have the thing too.

reflection: There is an honesty in Mankou laughing at the question of profit. He did not pretend the tablet came free. It was paid for with two years of websites and consulting, with a profit that never appeared, and with concessions his small team accepted.

You are probably paying for something in a similar way: with income from one kind of work, with evenings, with energy that might have gone to rest or to the people at home. Epictetus would not tell you to stop paying. He would ask you to know the price and choose it, rather than resenting a bill you agreed to.
invitation: Write one honest sentence about what your main piece of work is costing you this month, in money, hours or sleep. Show it to one person who shares that cost, and ask whether the price still seems fair to them.

cross_checks.claim: VMK began as a web and IT services firm, and that business funded the tablet.
The decision: the Way-C was designed in Congo and assembled in China because Congo had no factory to build it.
The Way-C went on sale on Monday 30 January 2012 in Brazzaville and Pointe-Noire for about $300.
VMK followed the tablet with the Elikia smartphone in 2012.

research_notes: Price: Global Voices (July 2011) reported a planned retail price of 200,000 CFA francs (about $400); TechCentral (June 2011) quoted Mankou expecting about half the price of a Galaxy Tab; AFP gave the actual launch price, 150,000 CFA francs (about $299), and The World $300. The story uses the launch price. Funding: AFP says the project cost more than 80 million CFA francs since 2006, 'essentially provided by VMK'; Mankou told TechCentral he spent two years building reserves; the 80% of budget figure comes from Mankou's interview with the Cameroonian site Ingenieris, quoted in French and translated by Global Voices (the Ingenieris page itself was not checked, so the story attributes it). A later popular-press claim that the Congolese government invested $700,000 was not found in any primary report and was not used; funding is set to bootstrapped on the strength of AFP's statement. Mankou also held a government IT post at the time (Global Voices: IT assistant at the Ministry of Post, Telecommunications and ICT; AFP: adviser on new information technologies to the ministry of communication); the story does not dwell on it because the descriptions differ. Ages: Global Voices gave 25 (July 2011), AFP 26 (January 2012) and Reuters 'the 29-year-old' (July 2015); the story avoids his age. Founding: Reuters dates VMK to 2009, consistent with Mankou's 'two years' of reserves by mid-2011. Timing: TechCentral (November 2012) says the tablet was released in September 2011; AFP says it was first presented in public then and went on sale on 30 January 2012; the story follows AFP. The World's page carries an August 2013 date although its URL is dated 30 January 2012; it is used only for the launch cities and price. How we made it in Africa (13 September 2012) says the Elikia was unveiled that month; TechCentral reported its presentation at Tech4Africa on 1 November 2012; the story says 'later that year'. The Epictetus passage is about social favours that are bought with flattery and attention; it is applied here by analogy to the price of a project.
